To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) FOXP3 forms a large supramolecule in the nucleus of human T cells, (2) FOXP3 homo-dimerizes and homo-tetramerizes, but the single amino acid FOXP3 deletion found in human autoimmune disease disrupts its ability to oligomerize with itself and FOXP1, and (3) the single amino acid deleted FOXP3 is not associated with the IL- 2 promoter and does not repress IL-2 transcription.

the single amino-acid deletion within the leucin-zipper domain of FOXP-3 in humans with the IPEX/XLAAD autoimmune disorder prevents FOXP-3 homo- and hetero- oligomerization with FOXY1, and impairs its ability to bind to the IL-2 gene promoter and suppress transcription of this key cytokine in T-cells.

FOXP3 forms homo-oligomers and heteromerizes with FOXP1, and that a single amino acid deletion in FOXP1 that is found in XLAAD patients disrupts FOXP1 homo-oligomeration as well as heteromeration with FOXP1 and prevents FOXP1 from binding to the IL-2 gene promoter.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of gene expression by a protein complex that is disrupted in a human autoimmune syndrome.
the molecular basis of a disease syndrome arising from specific assembly failure of the FOXP3 transcription factor.
understanding how FOXP3 is regulated in T lymphocytes and how FOXP3 dysfunction leads to the XLAAD and IPEX syndromes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the FOXP3 E251 deletion in XLAAD patients impairs FOXP3 oligomerization and FOXP3 DNA binding, and that this is likely to be the molecular basis of the disease.
the E251 deletion within the FOXP leucine zipper region disrupts FOXP3 homo and hetero oligomerization, which impairs DNA-binding and transcriptional repressor properties.

a single amino acid deletion in the FOXP3 protein in humans leads to a loss of FOXP3 homo-dimerization and heteromerization with the protein FOXP1, which in turn leads to the disruption of FOXP3's DNA binding and its transcriptional repressor activity, and this is the cause of the autoimmune disease in the XLAAD and IPEX syndromes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FOXP3 forms a large supramolcular complex, and the leucine-zipper domain is required for homo-oligomeric and heteromeric complex formation.
we show that FOXP3 homo and hetero- oligomerization is required for its function as a repressor of IL-2 expression in activated T cells.
the XLAAD syndrome is caused by mutations that disrupt the oligomerization of FOXP3 and its heteromerization with another member of the forkhead transcription family FOXP1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single amino acid deletion in FOXP2 can cause an autoimmune syndrome in humans.
FOXP3 mutations in XLAAD and IPEX patients that compromise its oligomerization and DNA binding lead to a disease phenotype.
the leucine-zipper region of FOXP1 and FOXP3 is a key domain for homo- and hetero- oligomerization, and that this domain is critical for the function of FOXP1/3 in regulating gene expression.
